name: HMS Victory
fate: Preserved in dry dock at Portsmouth; still a commissioned Royal Navy ship
description: Nelson's flagship at the Battle of Trafalgar on 21 October 1805, where the Royal Navy defeated the combined French and Spanish fleets and Nelson was fatally wounded on her quarterdeck.
fun_fact: In dry dock since 1922, she is the oldest naval vessel in the world still in commission.
image_credit: Photo: Cimosteve / MARC912374 · CC0

name: USS Constitution
fate: Still in commission; berthed at the Charlestown Navy Yard, Boston
description: One of the first six frigates built for the United States Navy. In the War of 1812 she defeated HMS Guerriere, HMS Java and other British warships, becoming a national symbol.
fun_fact: She became "Old Ironsides" in 1812, when British shot was seen bouncing off her live-oak hull. She is the oldest commissioned warship still afloat.
image_credit: Photo: U.S. Navy / Seaman Matthew R. Fairchild · Public domain

name: RMS Titanic
fate: Sank in the North Atlantic on 15 April 1912
description: The largest ship afloat when she entered service. On her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York she struck an iceberg late on 14 April 1912 and sank in under three hours; more than 1,500 people died.
fun_fact: Only three of her four funnels served the boilers. The fourth was added largely for appearance and was used for ventilation.
image_credit: Photo: F. G. O. Stuart, 1912 · Public domain

name: HMS Dreadnought
fate: Sold for scrap in 1921 and broken up
description: The first "all-big-gun" battleship and the first with steam turbines. She made every earlier battleship obsolete almost overnight and gave her name to a whole generation of warships.
fun_fact: Her only kill was the German submarine U-29, rammed and sunk in March 1915 — the only time a battleship is known to have sunk a submarine.
image_credit: Photo: U.S. Naval Historical Center, NH 61017 · Public domain

name: USS Enterprise (CV-6)
fate: Decommissioned in 1947; scrapped 1958–1960 despite efforts to preserve her
description: The most decorated American warship of the Second World War, with 20 battle stars. She fought at Midway, the Eastern Solomons, Santa Cruz, the Philippine Sea and Leyte Gulf.
fun_fact: Japan announced her sunk on three separate occasions, which helped earn her the nickname "The Grey Ghost".
image_credit: Photo: U.S. Navy, 1945 · Public domain

name: Yamato
fate: Sunk by US carrier aircraft north of Okinawa, 7 April 1945
description: With her sister Musashi, the heaviest and most powerfully armed battleship ever built: about 72,000 tonnes at full load, carrying nine 46 cm (18.1 in) guns, the largest ever mounted on a warship.
fun_fact: Each of her three main gun turrets weighed around 2,500 tonnes — roughly as much as a destroyer of the period.
image_credit: Photo: Hasuya Hirohata, 1941 · Public domain

name: Bismarck
fate: Sunk in the North Atlantic on 27 May 1941
description: Germany's most famous battleship. On 24 May 1941 she sank HMS Hood in the Denmark Strait; a vast Royal Navy hunt followed, and a torpedo from a Swordfish biplane jammed her rudder.
fun_fact: Her wreck was found in 1989, nearly 4,800 metres down, by Robert Ballard — the oceanographer who had located Titanic four years earlier.
image_credit: Photo: Bundesarchiv, Bild 193-04-1-26 · CC BY-SA 3.0 DE

name: HMS Hood
fate: Sunk by Bismarck on 24 May 1941; only 3 of 1,418 crew survived
description: For two decades the largest warship in the world and the pride of the Royal Navy, known as "The Mighty Hood". She blew up minutes into her engagement with Bismarck in the Denmark Strait.
fun_fact: In 1923–24 she led the "Empire Cruise", a ten-month voyage around the world covering more than 38,000 nautical miles.
image_credit: Photo: Allan C. Green, 1924; restored by Adam Cuerden · Public domain

name: USS Missouri
fate: Decommissioned in 1992; museum ship at Pearl Harbor since 1999
description: The last battleship commissioned by the United States. Japan's surrender was signed on her deck in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945, ending the Second World War. She later served in Korea and the 1991 Gulf War.
fun_fact: She is moored facing the wreck of USS Arizona, so the two ships mark the beginning and the end of America's war in the Pacific.
image_credit: Photo: U.S. Navy, 80-G-453331, 1944 · Public domain

name: HMS Belfast
fate: Museum ship on the River Thames, London, since 1971
description: A Royal Navy cruiser that helped sink Scharnhorst at the Battle of North Cape in 1943, bombarded the Normandy beaches on D-Day and later fought in the Korean War.
fun_fact: Her forward guns are trained on a motorway service station on the M1, about 12 miles away, to show how far they could reach.
image_credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 3.0

name: USS Arizona
fate: Sunk at Pearl Harbor, 7 December 1941; her wreck is a national memorial
description: A battleship destroyed in the attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, when a bomb detonated her forward magazines. 1,177 of her crew were killed, almost half of all those who died in the attack.
fun_fact: Oil still seeps from the wreck more than 80 years later. The drops rising to the surface are known as the "tears of the Arizona".
image_credit: Photo: U.S. National Archives, NARA 5900075 · Public domain

name: Cutty Sark
fate: Preserved in dry dock at Greenwich, London, since 1954
description: One of the last and fastest tea clippers. The Suez Canal opened the same month she was launched, handing the tea trade to steamships, but she later set record passages carrying wool from Australia.
fun_fact: Her name comes from Robert Burns's poem Tam o' Shanter: a "cutty sark" is the short shift worn by the witch Nannie, who is her figurehead.
image_credit: Photo: Ethan Doyle White · CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Vasa
fate: Sank in Stockholm harbour on 10 August 1628; raised in 1961
description: Built for King Gustavus Adolphus as one of the most heavily armed ships of her day. Dangerously top-heavy, she heeled over in a gust and sank barely 1,300 metres into her maiden voyage.
fun_fact: After 333 years on the seabed she was raised almost intact. About 98 per cent of the ship on display in Stockholm is original.
image_credit: Photo: JavierKohen · CC BY-SA 3.0

name: Santa María
fate: Wrecked off Hispaniola on 25 December 1492
description: Flagship of Christopher Columbus on his first voyage across the Atlantic in 1492, and the largest of his three ships alongside the caravels Niña and Pinta. Her timbers were salvaged to build the settlement of La Navidad.
fun_fact: No plans or reliable pictures of her survive, so every replica — like the one photographed here around 1904 — is an educated guess.
image_credit: Photo of a replica, c. 1904: Library of Congress · Public domain

name: HMS Endeavour
fate: Scuttled off Newport, Rhode Island, in 1778 as the transport Lord Sandwich
description: The ship of James Cook's first voyage of discovery (1768–1771), which observed the transit of Venus from Tahiti, circumnavigated New Zealand and charted the east coast of Australia.
fun_fact: NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavour was named after her, which is why its name uses the British spelling.
image_credit: Painting: Samuel Atkins, c. 1794 · National Library of Australia · Public domain

name: USS Nautilus (SSN-571)
fate: Decommissioned in 1980; museum ship at Groton, Connecticut
description: The world's first nuclear-powered submarine. She first put to sea in January 1955 with the signal "Underway on nuclear power", and in 1958 became the first vessel to reach the North Pole, passing beneath the ice.
fun_fact: President Harry Truman laid her keel in 1952, and First Lady Mamie Eisenhower christened her at the launch in 1954.
image_credit: Photo: U.S. Navy · Public domain

name: HMS Warrior
fate: Restored 1979–1985; museum ship at Portsmouth since 1987
description: Britain's first iron-hulled, armoured warship, built in answer to the French ironclad Gloire. The largest, fastest and most powerful warship of her day, she never fired a shot in anger.
fun_fact: Before her restoration she spent fifty years as a floating oil jetty at Pembroke Dock in Wales.
image_credit: Photo: Geni · CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Scharnhorst
fate: Sunk at the Battle of North Cape, 26 December 1943; 36 of 1,968 crew survived
description: A fast German capital ship that raided Atlantic shipping with her sister Gneisenau, sank the carrier HMS Glorious in 1940 and broke through the English Channel in the 1942 "Channel Dash".
fun_fact: While sinking HMS Glorious she scored a hit at about 24 km (26,000 yards) — one of the longest-range naval gunnery hits ever recorded.
image_credit: Photo: Bundesarchiv, DVM 10 Bild-23-63-07 · CC BY-SA 3.0 DE

name: Akagi
fate: Crippled at the Battle of Midway, 4 June 1942, and scuttled the next day
description: Flagship of the Japanese carrier striking force that attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941. Six months later she was hit by American dive bombers at Midway and burned out of control.
fun_fact: Laid down as a battlecruiser, she was first completed as a carrier with three flight decks stacked one above another, and later rebuilt with one.
image_credit: Photo: Imperial Japanese Navy, 1941 (NH 73059) · Public domain

name: RMS Queen Mary
fate: Retired in 1967; now a hotel and museum at Long Beach, California
description: Cunard's great Atlantic express liner. She held the Blue Riband for the fastest crossing from 1938 to 1952, and as a wartime troopship she relied on her speed to outrun U-boats.
fun_fact: In July 1943 she carried 16,683 people on a single crossing — still the most ever transported on one ship.
image_credit: Photo: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress · Public domain

name: Mikasa
fate: Preserved as a memorial ship at Yokosuka since 1926
description: Built in Britain by Vickers, she was Admiral Togo's flagship at the Battle of Tsushima in May 1905, where the Japanese fleet destroyed Russia's Baltic Fleet in one of history's most decisive naval battles.
fun_fact: She is the last surviving pre-dreadnought battleship anywhere in the world.
image_credit: Photo: unknown photographer, 1905 · Public domain

name: Aurora
fate: Museum ship in Saint Petersburg since 1957
description: A survivor of the Battle of Tsushima. On 7 November 1917 (25 October, Old Style) a blank shot from her bow gun signalled the storming of the Winter Palace, the start of the October Revolution.
fun_fact: During the Siege of Leningrad her guns were taken ashore to defend the city and the ship was sunk in shallow water. She was raised in 1944.
image_credit: Photo: Никонико962 · CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Fram
fate: Preserved at the Fram Museum in Oslo since 1936
description: Built for Fridtjof Nansen's attempt to drift across the Arctic in the pack ice, and later used by Otto Sverdrup and by Roald Amundsen, who sailed her south for his journey to the South Pole in 1911.
fun_fact: Her rounded hull was designed so that squeezing ice would lift her instead of crushing her. She is said to have sailed farther north and south than any other wooden ship.
image_credit: Photo: from Amundsen, The South Pole (1912), via NOAA · Public domain

name: Georgios Averof
fate: Museum ship at Palaio Faliro, near Athens, since 1984
description: Flagship of the Greek fleet in the Balkan Wars. Under Admiral Kountouriotis she led the victories at Elli and Lemnos in 1912–13 that secured Greek control of the Aegean.
fun_fact: About a third of her cost was paid from the bequest of the benefactor George Averoff. She is the only armoured cruiser that survives today.
image_credit: Photo: Cmfrangos · CC BY 4.0
